summary: A belated report on a network meeting, written by Vint Cerf in 1970. It records what was discussed rather than defining a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 63 reports on a Network Working Group meeting at Lincoln Labs about host-to-host messages and records. It records decisions on where records may begin and how an eight-bit type identifies their contents.

subtitle: Decisions on record formats from a May 1970 Network Working Group meeting.

tldr.problem: The group needed to record decisions about message and record formats for Host-Host information exchange.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 63 reports that records may begin anywhere in a message, reserve their first eight bits for type information, and use assigned types for data representations.
tldr.outcome: The document is a meeting report that records decisions and attendees, not a complete protocol specification.

sections.title: The Lincoln Labs Meeting
sections.content:
Vint Cerf's report describes a Network Working Group meeting hosted at Lincoln Labs on May 8, 1970. Topics included Lincoln Lab's Local Interaction Language, records and message formats for Host-Host exchange, and miscellaneous issues.

The meeting discussed RFC 42's proposal to precede messages with an 8-bit type byte.
sections.plainLanguage: The report summarizes a meeting about interactive systems and host-to-host message formats. Much of its detail concerns the type information at the start of a record.

sections.title: Record Boundaries and Type Bytes
sections.content:
The attendees agreed that records may begin anywhere within a message, and that the first 8 bits of a record are reserved for type information. The first transmission on a connection starts a record.

Type 0 indicates an arbitrarily long record with no further type bytes. Types 1, 2, and 3 identify 8-bit ASCII, EBCDIC, and MOD 33 TTY 7-bit ASCII. Types 4 and 5 identify local forms followed by another type byte.
sections.plainLanguage: A record can begin within a message and starts with an eight-bit type. The type identifies the data representation that follows.

sections.title: Messages, Records, and Attribution
sections.content:
The report distinguishes messages from records: message receipt has no semantic importance by itself, while a received record may start an interpretation process.

It lists the meeting attendees and notes that Jim Torson would receive NWG/RFCs instead of Chuck Rose at Case University.
sections.plainLanguage: A message boundary does not itself tell a program what to do. A record's type and contents may be meaningful to the receiving program.

references.text: NWG/RFC 42, proposal discussed at the meeting concerning message type bytes.
